control_ladder.note_beginner: When a clump goes streaky and papery, cut it right down to the base and carry the trimmings out of the garden. The insects leave with the blades you take off, and chives push up fresh green leaves that start clean.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A hard shear to the base is the reset for a marked clump: it carries the resident population out with the foliage and forces clean regrowth. Remove what you cut rather than leaving it at the edge of the bed, and treat it as the first move in a heavy year rather than the last.

control_ladder.note_beginner: A jet from the hose knocks thrips loose while numbers are still low. Point it down into the crease where the blades overlap, because they feed tucked in there rather than out on the open leaf. Do it in the morning so the foliage has the day to dry.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Thrips sit down in the leaf axils, the folds where blade meets stem, which is why a directed water pass reaches them when a general wetting does not. Use it as the physical knock-down under light pressure, in the morning so leaf wetness does not carry into the evening.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Lacewings and minute pirate bugs, two small helpful insects that feed on thrips, do steady work on a chive clump. Leave them room by holding off on broad insect sprays, which take them out along with the pest.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Conserving the resident predators, minute pirate bugs and lacewings among them, is the standing control on a crop where the feeding damage is usually cosmetic. A broad-spectrum material costs more here than the streaking does, since it removes the enemies holding the population flat.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If streaking keeps spreading after the water and the shear, insecticidal soap on the leaves is the next step. It works only where it lands, so wet the folds the thrips are sitting in. Give harvested blades a rinse before they go in the kitchen.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap is a contact material and the leaf axils are the hard part of the coverage, so a pass that misses the folds misses much of the population. It can burn foliage above 90°F or on a drought-stressed clump, which is the same hot, dry weather thrips build in, so water first and spray in the cool part of the day. Rinse harvested leaves.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Spinosad is a stronger organic spray, worth considering only in a bad year that has run past soap. It is hard on bees while it is fresh, so spray at dusk and keep it off a clump in flower, since chive blooms draw bees and hoverflies.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Spinosad is the material chives' guidance names alongside soap for a year when pressure warrants it, and it stands behind the physical and cultural steps rather than in place of them. It is toxic to bees when sprayed and for roughly a day afterward, so a dusk pass on a clump that is out of bloom, or one whose flower stalks have been cut, is the condition for using it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Put a new chive planting on ground that has not just carried alliums, the onion family that chives, onions, garlic and leeks belong to. Starting away from a spot that was mined last season cuts what carries over into the new plants.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Siting a new planting away from allium ground that was mined recently lowers what carries over into it. The fly works two flights a year against the same host group, so ground it has already found presents the same target in spring and again in fall.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Any blade carrying a wavy pale tunnel, or the line of white dots punched down it, should come off the plant and go out with the trash rather than onto the ground beside the bed. The maggots, and the brown seed-shaped pupae that are the resting stage between maggot and adult, sit inside that tissue at the leaf bases. Clear plant debris off the bed too.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Mined foliage carries the larvae, and the puparia lodge in the leaf sheaths, so stripping it removes the developing generation rather than tidying the clump. Sanitize crop residue on the same pass, and destroy what you take off. Larval wounds also open the way for secondary bacterial and fungal rots, which is a second reason not to leave mined leaves standing.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Floating row cover is a sheet of light fabric you drape over the planting; sun and rain pass through it and insects do not. Put it on in early spring and again in fall, the two stretches when the flies are out, so they cannot land on the leaves to lay eggs. Tuck the edges down.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Exclusion is the primary control and its value is in the timing: cover ahead of the spring flight, roughly March into May, and again for the fall flight, September into October, rather than after the rows of white feeding punctures appear. Seal the edges, and lay it over ground that did not grow alliums last season so the cover does not hold emerging flies in with the crop.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Where the flies are heavy, spinosad is a stronger organic spray that can help. It is hard on bees while fresh, so spray at dusk and keep it off plants in flower.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Spinosad is what chives' guidance names for high pressure, standing behind exclusion and sanitation rather than replacing them. It is toxic to bees when sprayed and for about a day afterward, so a dusk application on a planting that is out of bloom is the condition for using it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Do not set a new chive planting, or other onion-family crops, back into a spot that has just carried them. The flies build up where alliums repeat, so a fresh bed starts the plants away from that.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: The fly overwinters as pupae in the soil of allium ground, so moving a new planting off that ground separates it from the generation emerging there in spring. Rotation and residue cleanup are the pair that carries this problem, because no organic rescue reaches larvae already in the crown.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Clear out old bulbs, culls and onion-family debris instead of leaving them around the bed, since that material is what draws the flies in to lay eggs. If a clump's crown is already riddled and rotting, pull it and destroy it, because it will not come back from that.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Culls and residue are the lure for egg-laying, so stripping them takes away the attractant rather than the insect. Rogue out plants with a rotted crown and destroy them. An established clump is seldom lost outright, but it can be set back, and the damage runs worst in cool, moist springs where debris has accumulated.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Floating row cover is a sheet of light fabric draped over the planting, and it stops the flies from reaching the base of the plant where they lay their eggs. Get it on early in spring and weight the edges down so nothing walks in underneath.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Cover early in spring and seal the edges: eggs go in at the plant base, so the barrier is worth what its seal is worth. Lay it on ground that did not grow alliums last season, since pupae overwintering in that soil can emerge under the cover and be held there with the crop.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep the nitrogen feeding light. Nitrogen is the nutrient that drives leafy growth, and aphids multiply fastest on soft new growth, so a restrained hand gives them less to work with.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Restrained nitrogen is preventive rather than corrective, since heavy feeding produces the flushes of soft growth colonies exploit. On chives it is a habit worth keeping rather than a response, because what shows up here is sporadic and minor.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Wash a colony off with a strong spray of water. On chives that is usually all that is called for, and it costs the helpful insects nothing. Spray in the morning so the blades dry off.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A water jet handles the occasional colony without touching the predators working the clump. Chives are among the least aphid-prone herbs, and their sulfur compounds make an inhospitable host, so treat a colony as an event to knock back rather than a season-long program.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Ladybugs, lacewings and hoverflies all eat aphids, and a chive clump left to flower feeds the hoverflies as well. Letting them work is usually enough here, so hold off on broad sprays that take them out too.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Conservation is close to the whole program on this crop. The umbels, the round flower heads chives carry when they bloom, feed hoverflies, so a planting allowed to flower supports the predators that keep colonies from persisting.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Insecticidal soap is there for a colony that keeps building, though on chives it is seldom needed. It works by contact, so it has to wet the insects, and it also hits soft-bodied helpful insects it lands on. Give what you cut a rinse before you cook with it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Soap is warranted rarely here. It is a contact material that also kills the soft-bodied beneficials it wets, so confine a pass to the colonized scapes, the flower stalks, rather than treating the clump. Skip it on a drought-stressed plant or above 90°F, where it can burn foliage, and rinse harvested leaves.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Give clumps room, and split crowded ones, so air moves through the leaves. This disease runs where damp foliage stays damp, and a stand that dries quickly is a poorer place for it.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Dividing crowded clumps and spacing them shortens the leaf wetness this oomycete depends on. It favors cool, humid weather, below about 75°F, and a dense stand holds exactly those conditions, so the layout decision is made before the weather arrives rather than in response to it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Site chives where water drains away and the sun reaches them. Soggy, shaded ground holds the dampness this disease needs, and a crowded planting on wet ground is where it spreads fastest.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Poorly drained ground holds the moisture that sustains the pathogen, so drainage and exposure are worth settling before a clump goes in. On heavy or low-lying ground, correct that first rather than leaning on the practices further along.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Deliver the water down at the soil line and keep it off the foliage. Wet blades and splashing water are how this one travels, so watering low takes away part of its route.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Basal irrigation removes the splash route and holds leaf wetness to what the weather imposes. The pathogen moves on wind and splashing water and needs long wet periods, so this is the practice half of the defense that spacing sets at planting.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Take off affected leaves as you notice them, and if a clump is badly hit, cut it to the base so it regrows once the weather turns drier. Get the cuttings out of the garden.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Strip infected foliage, and shear a heavily affected clump so the regrowth comes on under drier conditions. Once it is established the home garden has no reliable cure, which is what puts the weight on removing tissue and on the cultural steps above.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Thin crowded plantings and divide clumps so air can move between the leaves. Rust does the most in damp, crowded stands, and room is what lets the blades dry.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Open the stand by dividing and spacing. Moisture and crowding are the two conditions the guidance names for this one, so a layout that dries quickly works on both at once.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Hold the fertilizer back, nitrogen especially. Lush, over-fed growth carries rust worse, and heavy feeding also thickens the clump back into the crowding you just opened up.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Heavy nitrogen is one of the three conditions this disease is tied to, along with crowding and moisture. Lush growth is more rust-prone and it also closes the stand back up, so restrained feeding and open spacing are one decision rather than two.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Keep the hose at soil level instead of sprinkling the clump from above. Overhead watering leaves the blades wet, and damp foliage is what this fungus wants.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Skip overhead irrigation. The spores travel on air, so this does not shut off arrival; what it does is hold leaf wetness to what the weather brings instead of adding to it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Cut off leaves carrying the orange spots and destroy them, or shear the whole clump to the base so it comes back clean. Doing it early, before the spots spread, is the point.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: A hard cut to the base takes the pustules off with the foliage and the clump regrows clean. Clear the debris as well, and act before heavy infection yellows the blades and dies them back. At garden scale a spray is seldom called for here.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Start with clean plants from a source you trust, and do not bring in soil from a garden that has had this disease. An affected spot cannot be cured, so what you settle before planting counts for far more than anything you do afterward.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Clean, sclerotia-free stock is the decision made before anything reaches the ground, and it carries the weight here because there is no rescue for an infested site. Sclerotia are the fungus's resting bodies, and they are what a dirty division or a scoop of imported soil brings with it.

control_ladder.note_beginner: If a spot has had white rot, keep chives, onions and garlic out of it and put new onion-family plants on fresh ground. What the fungus leaves in the soil is a scatter of hard black survival bodies the size of poppy seeds, and they wait there for many years until another allium arrives.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Long rotation is the standing management, and its length comes from the sclerotia, which persist for many years and can leave a site unusable for alliums for a decade or more. Treat infested ground as quarantined from the onion family rather than as a bed on a rotation clock.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Dig out affected plants along with the soil around their roots and destroy them, since they will not recover. Keep that soil out of clean beds, and clean the dirt off your tools before you work elsewhere, because this fungus rides along on soil.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Rogue affected plants with the surrounding soil, and treat the soil itself as a thing that moves: tools, transplants and imported garden soil of unknown history are the routes into clean ground. Sanitation here is containment rather than cure, which is what makes it a standing habit instead of a response.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Divide crowded clumps and give the plants space so air moves through them. This gray mold gets its start in humid, crowded plantings where the leaves stay damp.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Open the stand at planting and keep it open by dividing. A dense canopy and the leaf wetness it holds are the conditions this one wants, so spacing acts on both at once and it is the step that costs nothing later.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Aim the water at the ground under the clump, not across the leaves, and do it early in the day so the blades dry before evening. Splashing is how this mold gets around, and a blade that stays wet is where it settles in.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Irrigate at the soil line and early: splashing water carries the spores and leaf wetness is what lets them establish. Watering low removes the splash route, and watering early shortens the wet period that dew and weather still impose.

control_ladder.note_beginner: Pick off spotted leaves, or shear the clump so it regrows clean, and clear away dead and dying foliage. Old tissue left in the clump is where this mold builds up.
control_ladder.note_seasoned: Cull spotted foliage or reset the clump with a hard shear, and strip senescing leaves, which the guidance names as the material to remove to cut inoculum. A home chive planting seldom calls for a spray, so the removal is the working control rather than a preliminary to one.
